Definition: Whether the digital ID credential serves as legal proof of an individual's identity as codified in law
Comments: The national ID card (bilhete de identidade) issued by DGRN serves as legal proof of identity and is accepted for voter registration, tax NIF, driving licence, and other official purposes. The World Bank foundational ID assessment confirms ID and birth certificates are used as legal identity documents across public administration. Scored 2 (Yes).
redteam_note: Only one source for a substantive score — corroborate.
revision_notes: Confirmed after full read of the World Bank ID4D Diagnostic (2023). The report lists the ID card as mandatory to open a bank account, activate a SIM, access basic health services and public assistance programmes, and cites Constitution Art.24 (right to identity) and the 1971 Civil Identification Law as its legal basis. Score of 2 (Yes) retained; scale is binary so no finer distinction possible.

Definition: Whether identity records are stored in electronic/digital format versus paper-based records
Comments: The World Bank foundational ID assessment confirms a centralised digital ID database is hosted at DGRN headquarters in Sao Tome (with local backup), and civil registration is managed through SIGA (hosted at University of Aveiro, Portugal). Both are digital databases. Birth data from 1920-2010 has been digitised and indexed. Scored 3 (Digital).
redteam_note: Only one source for a substantive score — corroborate.
revision_notes: Revised down from 3 to 2 after full read of the source. The same report states the identification card is 'a physical document with no electronic elements' and that only around 90,000 individuals were actually registered in the digital ID database (Oct 2021), against a DGRN claim that ~80% of the population (5+) hold an ID card — meaning most legacy paper-based ID holders are not yet in the digital database. This is a mix of paper and digital, not fully digital.

Definition: Whether credential is accepted or mandatory for accessing public healthcare services
Comments: The World Bank assessment notes the cédula pessoal/national ID is used for basic health services and was used for COVID-19 vaccination registration. Birth registration is conducted at hospitals. Free public healthcare is available to citizens. ID is required/used for health service access but not confirmed as strictly mandatory for all healthcare. Scored 2 (Accepted, not mandatory).
redteam_note: Only one source for a substantive score — corroborate.
revision_notes: Revised up from 2 to 3. The World Bank ID4D Diagnostic (2023) explicitly states the ID card 'is mandatory to access' basic public health services (an equivalent document, the cédula pessoal, also works) and to register for the COVID vaccine. This is direct evidence of a mandatory requirement, not merely acceptance.

Definition: Whether non-nationals including refugees, asylum seekers, and permanent residents are eligible to register
Comments: The World Bank assessment notes the ID system is 'open to all nationals and Santomean diaspora' and that civil registration covers nationals and foreigners born in STP. SIM registration and banking KYC accept passports (allowing non-nationals to use foreign documents). No evidence that non-nationals can obtain the STP national ID card, but some identity services (civil registration, SIM, banking) are accessible with foreign documents. Scored 2 (Some).
redteam_note: Only one source for a substantive score — corroborate.
revision_notes: Revised down from 2 to 1. The source is explicit that the foundational ID system is 'open to all nationals and Santomean diaspora' and that 'registration to obtain a national ID card is mandatory for all nationals... São Tomé and Príncipe nationality is a requirement.' There is no route for non-nationals (refugees, asylum seekers, permanent residents) to register in the ID system itself; other bodies accepting foreign passports for KYC is a separate matter of alternative documents, not ID-system eligibility, so this does not support a score of 'Some'.

Definition: Percentage of eligible population that has been issued or registered with digital ID credentials
Comments: The World Bank foundational ID assessment reports approximately 90,000 ID entries (2021) and the DGRN claims ~80% of the population aged 5+ holds an ID. With a total population of ~220,000, this implies roughly 50-60% overall population coverage (excluding young children). 30,539 ID cards were issued in 2022. Birth registration stands at 98%+ (2023). Scored 3 (50-69%).
redteam_note: Only one source for a substantive score — corroborate.
revision_notes: Revised down from 3 to 2. Original comment conflated two different figures in the same source: the DGRN's unverified claim that ~80% of the population hold a physical ID card, and the actual digital database count of only ~90,000 registrants (Oct 2021, ~40-45% of the ~219,000-240,000 population). Adding 2022 issuances (8,070 first-time cards) brings the database to roughly 98,000, still below 50% of even the eligible (5+) population. The report itself flags this gap, attributing it to legacy paper ID holders not yet entered in the digital database, so the higher DGRN figure is not reliable evidence of digital-ID coverage.

Definition: Whether credential is accepted or mandatory for registering for social assistance programs and accessing social services
Comments: The World Bank assessment confirms that social protection programmes (VFP, pensions; ~3,080 beneficiaries) use ID/civil documents for beneficiary registration in systems such as SIIPS/CORE-MIS. A National Social Protection Identification (NIS/NSIPI) is issued for the social registry. ID is accepted but the system has duplicate issues due to lack of a unique national ID. Scored 2 (Accepted, not yet fully mandatory/integrated).
redteam_note: Only one source for a substantive score — corroborate.
revision_notes: Revised up from 2 to 3. The source explicitly lists 'participate in government public assistance programs' among the uses for which the ID card is mandatory, and separately states the flagship Vulnerable Families Program 'mandates individuals to possess identification' (shared with the paying bank). A temporary NSIPI number exists as a workaround for people lacking documents, but the underlying requirement is mandatory rather than merely accepted.
